title: Data Breaches
objective: After this level you can explain what happens in a data breach, using Equifax in 2017, and connect it to the hashing and two-factor defenses.
summary: Equifax, 2017: an unpatched flaw let attackers in, unencrypted passwords opened 48 more databases, and data on 147 million people spilled. Hashing, a second factor and credit freezes help.

cards.headline: In 2017, one unpatched web page opened records on 147 million people.
cards.body: It wasn't a genius attack. A known flaw, a fix that never got installed, and a stash of passwords nobody had locked. Here's how the Equifax breach unfolded, and the defenses that make breaches like it less damaging.

events.label: A flaw in Apache Struts web software is announced; one portal misses the fix
Attackers break in through the online dispute portal
About 9,000 database queries go unnoticed for some 76 days

cards.headline: The passwords nobody locked
cards.body: Inside the portal, the attackers found usernames and passwords stored unencrypted. Those let them reach 48 more databases beyond the portal's 3. They took names, dates of birth and Social Security numbers, sending the data out in small encrypted pieces that looked like normal traffic.

cards.headline: Defenses that shrink the damage
cards.body: NIST's guidelines require services to store passwords only salted and hashed, scrambled one way so a stolen copy can't simply be read back. With multi-factor authentication, a thief holding your password still can't meet the second requirement. And for you in the US, a credit freeze is free and stops new credit being opened in your name.

cards.headline: Breach: dissected
learned: An unpatched flaw let attackers into Equifax in 2017
Hashed passwords and a second factor limit what a breach unlocks
A free credit freeze blocks new credit in your name

questions.prompt: Under NIST's guidelines, how should a service store your password?

options.label: In plain text, so it can email it back to you
options.rationale: Plain text is exactly what let the Equifax attackers in.

options.label: Salted and hashed, scrambled one way
In a cookie on your own browser
options.rationale: Passwords are checked by the service, not left in cookies.

options.label: As its ASCII codes
options.rationale: ASCII is just a public numbering of letters.

questions.explanation: NIST requires passwords to be salted and hashed, so a stolen copy can't simply be read back.

questions.prompt: How did the Equifax attackers reach 48 more databases after breaking into one web portal?

options.label: They guessed every password one at a time
They found usernames and passwords stored unencrypted
An employee emailed them the keys
options.rationale: The access came from stored credentials.

options.label: The databases had no passwords at all
options.rationale: The databases had passwords; the attackers found them unencrypted.

questions.explanation: Unencrypted credentials let the attackers move from the portal's 3 databases to 48 others.

questions.prompt: The Equifax passwords were stored unencrypted, as ordinary text codes. Given Level 4's ASCII, why could the attackers read them at once?

options.label: ASCII scrambles text, but only very weakly
options.rationale: ASCII doesn't scramble anything; it just numbers letters.

options.label: Passwords can't be stored as numbers at all
options.rationale: Everything in a computer is stored as numbers.

options.label: ASCII is a shared standard any computer can read back
The attackers had stolen Equifax's secret ASCII key
options.rationale: There is no key: the codebook is standard.

questions.explanation: ASCII gives letters standard numbers; any text program reads them back through the same codebook. Encoding hides nothing.
